REPUBLIC OF 
KAZAKHSTAN
2000 – 2004
UNDAF is jointly prepared by the UN Country Team and Government of Kazakhstan 
February 2000
TABLE OF CONTENTS
Foreword by the United Nations Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan
This United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) constitutes a significant step forward in co-ordinated development in Kazakhstan.  This UNDAF reflects the UN’s progress from increasingly effective but opportunistic co-ordination and collaboration into a comprehensive and more systematic strategic programme of action.  It consolidates UN Country Team efforts into a unified and unifying process.  It is the product of extensive consultations with Government, our development partners and stakeholders about needs and priorities.  It is based on understandings and agreements: between Government and the UN team as a whole, within theme groups involving other donors, and by Government’s approval of country strategies and programmes of our respective UN team members.  In addition, this UNDAF provides a mechanism and the framework for future activities by the Government and the UN Development System to improve cost-effectiveness, to exploit synergy, and to achieve greater positive impact on sustainable human development and growth. 
We mutually recognise and respect the mandates, resources and comparative advantages of each of our UN organisations and agencies.  We want each to succeed in its mission and goals in Kazakhstan.  However, we have concluded that general co-ordination and selective collaboration will enhance the impact beyond what can be accomplished by acting alone.
Our support for this principle is reinforced especially since 1997-8 by the growing success attained by the UN Country Team. On the ‘continuum of collaboration,’ the UN system has moved progressively along the scale from reactive harmonisation and ‘soft’ co-ordination at one end of the spectrum toward integrated initiatives and joint programmes and projects at the other end of the spectrum.  New programmes begin in 2000 with harmonised cycles for most of the UN’s funding organisations. The Country Team builds on concrete examples: physically joining in new common premises, more cost-effective common services; joint assessments (e.g., our Common Country Assessment of 1999, the jointly-formulated needs assessment and programme for the Semipalatinsk former nuclear testing region in response to the UN General Assembly’s Resolution), and joint programmes (e.g., integrated health, AIDS/drugs, formulation and implementation of women’s National Action Plan). 
Since 1993 when the United Nations Development System began providing assistance to Kazakhstan, the importance of co-ordinated development co-operation has been recognised and advocated as both a goal and practical necessity in order to optimise the use of limited resources, and enhance individual organisation’s impact.  The challenge has been how best to pursue this goal; and how best to harvest the fruits of improved collaboration.  The UNDAF is certainly not the end in itself.  It is a next step toward attaining effective collaboration; a practical tool for the UN Country Team and our partners.  We know that the tool must be used. We in the UN System in Kazakhstan are committed to exploit the potential within this Framework; periodically sharpening the tool and directing it toward the best opportunities for our collaboration and the highest priority socio-economic needs.   
This has been a real ‘team effort.’  I take this opportunity to thank especially my associates of the sixteen resident organisations and specialised agencies, and also the UN System’s non-residents, who are nonetheless represented, active and contribute to Country Team effectiveness. Special appreciation to Ms. Bakhyt Abdildina of UN/UNDP who helped bring us and the UNDAF together.  We invite comments and suggestions so that together we may improve the UN’s performance, relevance, cost-effectiveness and impact in Kazakhstan.
Herbert Behrstock
Introduction
The UN member States - both donors and recipient countries - have long sought progress and instruments to improve the effectiveness of UN operational activities for development. Many mechanisms have been used in the past decade, leading in July 1997 to the UN Secretary General’s reform proposals announced in his report “Renewing the United Nations: A Programme for Reform”. He has particularly emphasised that “in order to achieve goal-oriented collaboration, programmatic coherence and mutual reinforcement, the United Nations programmes of assistance should be formulated and presented as part of a single United Nations Development Assistance Framework”. The Guidelines for the UNDAF have been prepared by the United Nations Development Group based on resolutions by the UN General Assembly, ECOSOC, extensive UN system collaboration and the pilot results in eighteen countries. The main goal of the UNDAF is to serve as a common framework for UN development co-operation at level of each programme country. 
These global objectives challenged the UN Country Team to use this process and to improve its collaboration as reflected in the content of the Kazakhstan UNDAF. After a series of consultations with the government and other development partners it was agreed that the UNDAF would help the UN development system to better achieve the following: 
define priorities and collective actions for UN collaborative programming and implementation; 
harmonise individual programmes to become more effective; 
pursue global goals in support of national development challenges; 
achieve linkage with government’s national priorities and with partners in donor community; 
help the government to co-ordinate external assistance in these areas.  
The preparation of the UNDAF has involved all UN agencies represented in Kazakhstan, as well as some non-resident organisations through thematic groups’ consultations and regular Head of Agency meetings. Being totally in line with ongoing collaborative efforts of UN agencies in the country, the UNDAF formulation has officially started with the CCA as a needs assessment exercise. National strategies and policies, individual country programmes and other programme and evaluation documents were also used as a baseline for the UNDAF. 
The process in Kazakhstan built on regular consultations, a growing spirit of co-ordination and several concrete examples of collaboration and joint programmes and projects. With common themes identified and practical results already demonstrating the feasibility and advantages of co-operation the common programme framework for the next 5-year period was refined during the UN/Government Inter-Agency Retreat held outside Almaty on 28-29 May, 1999. This resulted in agreement about needs and opportunities for UN development co-operation and identified specific approaches for programme synergy. Members of the UN Country Team, having participated in laying the foundations for inter-agency collaboration at the project implementation levels, demonstrated a clear commitment to follow up. Senior government officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Health and Education, Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment Protection, National Commission on Family and Women Affairs, Agency for Strategic Planning and Agency for Economic Planning participated actively in the assessments and conclusions. Discussions were focused on the follow-up to global and national development agenda, thematic areas of co-operation and joint programming, and aid co-ordination.  
Draft revisions of the UNDAF have been circulated at various stages to the resident and non-resident agencies. Government has also provided feedback to the collective UN effort, to thematic group initiatives and plans, and to the endorsement or final approval of individual UN organisations’ and agencies’ programmes and participation in UN synergy. The final version was approved in February 2000. To facilitate the UNDAF implementation, it was agreed to have specific annual, mid-term and final monitoring and evaluation with participation from the UN Country Team, relevant Government institutions and donors. Benchmarks and related success indicators are to be introduced based on expected impact and the current situation for each major programme area proposed. Monthly Inter-Agency meetings and the Annual Resident Co-ordinator’s Report would also serve as a reporting instrument.       
Part 1.	Implications of Political, Social and Economic Trends for United Nations System Development Assistance.
Basic Facts about Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan is the second largest republic in the region of former Soviet Union and the ninth largest country in the world. Having a total area of some 2.7 million square kilometres it stretches 2800 kilometres east to west and 1600 kilometres north to south. The vast majority of Kazakhstan’s territory is plain land. Extensive rolling plains cover most of it surface, rising in the south-east towards the Central Asian massif and the mountain. The mountain systems of Tyan Shan, Jungar Alatau and Altai are located in the south-east of the country. The climate of Kazakhstan, typical of landlocked regions, is sharply continental and varies widely throughout the country. The summer temperatures are reaching above thirty degrees centigrade and in winter are falling to minus forty degrees in the north. The republic is divided into five geographic regions - Western, Eastern, Southern, Northern and Central Kazakhstan - and 14 administrative divisions (oblasts) (see Map 1.1).

 Land area	Total area of Kazakhstan is 2.7 million square kilometres
 Location	Central Asia. The country is bordered to the north, north-east and east by Russian Federation; to the south-east by China; and to the south by Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.

It is accepted that Almaty will continue as the financial and business centre of the country, as well as the interim base for international organisations, transport, communication and culture. In order to facilitate the development of the new capital, officially opened in June 1998, Astana was also given the status of a “special economic zone”.

According to the 1999 census, more than 14.9 million people live in Kazakhstan, of which 55,2 per cent in urban areas. Since the time of independence the number of constant population here decreased by almost two million from 16,8 million in 1991. As a consequence of socio-economic crisis, the number of population was mostly influenced by migration and by declining natural growth due to lower fertility and higher mortality rates. The average population density is low, 6 per square kilometres, compared to a European average of 67. Kazakhs are the main ethnic group of the Republic, whose share is 52% of population. The second largest ethnic group is Russians (31.3%). Average life expectancy in 1999 was 64 years. Almaty, the former capital of the Republic, has a population of 1.3 million. Astana, the new administrative capital, has a population of approximately 400,000, but is growing rapidly.

Administrative Divisions of the Republic of Kazakhstan
The political structure of the Republic of Kazakhstan is characterised as a Constitutional Republic with a strong presidency. With the adoption of the new Constitution in 1995, the presidency was given wide-ranging power over the legislature, judiciary and local government. The President, currently Mr. Nursultan Nazarbayev, is regarded as the Head of State, commander-in-chief of the armed forces and may veto legislation passed by the Parliament. The Parliament is the supreme representative body of the Republic. The Supreme Court represents the judicial branch of the state authority and the Government headed by the Prime Minister and appointed by the President represents the Executive power. 
1.2	Political and socio-economic performance since independence 
a) Governance and economic transition
The transformation process in Kazakhstan since 1991 was aimed initially at the structure of the government and public administration. Rapid progress in establishing the foundations of civil society eliminated former totalitarian models and developed democratic processes. At the same time, lacking the legal and technical foundations the reforms appeared not to be effective. The system of governance in Kazakhstan in practice was unnecessarily complicated and costly to maintain. To simplify the organisational structure, in March 1997 the number of ministries and state committees was reduced from 20 to 14 and from 12 to 2 respectively. Notwithstanding the Government’s efforts especially since establishment of the Agency for Public Service, the existing system of governance still suffers from frequent structural reorganisations and lack of coherence. Establishment of a compact and professional government, appropriate to market reforms and management methods, as well as creation of an effective legal framework have therefore become the major priorities for development. 
Regarding economic performance since independence, Kazakhstan has also passed through several stages. Starting from 1991 Kazakhstan has implemented various national programmes for economic transformation. Despite complicated economic and social conditions, the country managed to achieve macro-economic stabilisation. Inflation was reduced from 2,200% in 1993 to 11.3% in 1997 and 1.9% in 1998. The first year of real growth by 0.5 per cent was 1996. In 1997, this trend became stronger: the GDP volume increased by 1.7 percent. Nevertheless, economic growth in Kazakhstan was very uneven. Due to both domestic and external economic factors related to financial crisis in Russia and East Asia, by the end of 1998 GDP in Kazakhstan decreased by 2.5%, imposing further challenges to the economy, social security and human development. Floating of the exchange rate in May 1999 and tightened budgets were two of the first measures adopted to cope with these problems.  
b) Social development situation
Insufficient attention to social priorities during the economic and political transition, as well as limited resources of the country led to decline of human development of the population. Also relevant are the growing disparities and inequalities in income and standards of living. 
Quality of life of the population. In 1998 more than 43.4% (38.5% in towns and 47.7% in rural areas) of the population had available resources below the subsistence minimum.
Unemployment, especially among young people. In 1998 34.0% of those who registered with state employment services were aged 16-29 years. Official unemployment has reached 3.7% but most alarming is the “hidden unemployment”. According to the national statistics, the general (actual) unemployment level was 13.1% in 1998 and was especially high in small towns reaching 30-40% of the economically active population. 
Social protection of the population. Financial difficulties led to the establishing stricter eligibility criteria for the allocation of state support for low-income citizens. Thus, in 1997-1998 allowances for single mothers, and some pension benefits were lifted.
Demographic indicators. Although the infant mortality rate is in a steady decrease, the maternal mortality ratio continues to rise and reached to 77.5 per 100,000 live births in 1998. Birth rate in Kazakhstan is the lowest of the Central Asian Republics and between 1991-1998 it declined from 21.5 to 14.4 per 1,000. The life expectancy has also declined since 1989 by 3.2 years and reached 64 year in 1998. Ongoing out-migration is occurring in industrially developed oblasts, especially in Eastern and Northern Kazakhstan. 
Health of population. Since 1997, TB cases notification increased by 26 per cent and TB mortality by 9 per cent. The rate for hepatitis, after falling slightly in 1991-1994, returned to a figure close to the average for the Central Asian Republics and remains one of the highest in the European Region. In 1997-1998 the number of citizens testing HIV positive increased by 1.5 times. 
The level of education of the population. Total education coverage of the population aged 6-24 years declined from 65.4% in 1994 to 64.0% in 1998. Currently around half of rural schools are primary or incomplete secondary schools and this has inevitably led to a rise in the number of children with inadequate secondary education. 
The continuation of unfavourable social trends may in future result in a serious national problem of declining human potential, including reduced competitiveness of human resources on the world market, falling productivity and lower quality of commodities and services. In such conditions the role of the state increases enormously. 
c) Environment 
Kazakhstan possesses an enormous potential in natural resources able to provide for the long-term needs of the modest-sized population of this large Republic. At the same time, the country’s environment is very vulnerable, especially its water resource quality. As reaffirmed in the National Environment Action Plan, water supply has become a major problem mainly due to irrational development of irrigation based farming, as well as regulation of runoff in industrialised, mining and generally in arid climatic conditions. The Aral Sea water supply and stable utilisation of resources were destroyed in one generation. The problem of fresh water deficit (about 240 cubic meters of water per year per capita) is exacerbated by its low quality. According to the Sanitary and Epidemiological Service, 13% of water samples taken from surface water bodies do not meet hygienic standards. 
Kazakhstan is the only country in the world, which has consistently undergone nuclear testing for almost 40 years. About 470 nuclear tests resulting in release of 45 million curies of radiation into the atmosphere have been conducted in this region since 1949. Although in the late 1980s the local anti-nuclear movement and politics combined successfully for the closure of the Semipalatinsk nuclear testing site, toxins and pollutants had enormous consequences and continue their terrible impact on the people, environment and economy. 
Following the General Assembly’s resolution, in mid-1998 the UN Country team including UNDP, UNICEF, UNESCO, UNFPA, IAEA, ILO, OCHA, UNIDO and WHO carried an assessment mission to help the government of Kazakhstan to assess the consequences of the nuclear testing. USD43 million prioritised package of the Relief and Rehabilitation Programme was then presented at the 1999 International Conference in Tokyo. As a reflection of international interest and concern, more than $20 million was pledged from Japan, the General Board of Global Ministries, NATO, the World Bank and other UN organisations. A National Action Plan in the spheres of health, humanitarian aid, ecological rehabilitation, economic development and information dissemination is now being formulated by the Kazakh authorities for remedial measures.
Air pollution has also become a serious problem, especially for such industrial centres as Temirtau, Ekibastuz and Pavlodar. Major air pollution sources are fossil fuel electric power plants, mining and metallurgy. In Almaty, the largest city in the country, 90 % of total air pollution is produced by road transport. Kazakhstan also recognises the overall problem of sustainable land use and threats to longer-term desertification. The most “anti-environmental” industries like, for example, the oil and gas industry do not undertake adequate steps for complete utilisation of casing-head gas. In the regions of oil and gas extraction and oil refinery - Atyrau and Mangistau oblasts - work is conducted using obsolete technology and outdated equipment that bring about accidents and leakage of oil (the volume of spilt oil forms more than 5 million tones). As a result of Caspian Sea level rise, more than 200 oil wells and oil fields have become flooded that threaten not only biological diversity but the whole ecosystem of the Caspian Sea. 
Thus, it is clear that the ecological situation in Kazakhstan is very difficult. There are eight natural reservations, two national parks, and dozens of hunting reserves in Kazakhstan, the total area of which is 850,000 hectares, where no economic activities are allowed. But all together they occupy just 0.3% of the territory of the country. Given the fact of significant reduction in state-funded environmental services and, as a consequence, deterioration in the condition of purification facilities, as well as the long-standing apathy of a society preoccupied with social and economic problems, it could be concluded that the nature is preserved only by its inner reserves. 
1.3. National development priorities 
Since independence, there has been excellent progress in macroeconomics and general financial stability. Kazakhstan has introduced a convertible national currency, completed a large portion of its privatisation program, price and trade liberalisation, undertaken radical reform of pension system, financial services, legislation on foreign investment and public sector institutions. Despite unfavourable domestic and external conditions, the country managed to achieve stability and create prerequisites for future economic growth. However, the intensive efforts and implemented concepts and reforms have not reduced the decline in human development and have raised new complexities and doubts. Further development in the country was therefore focused on narrowing the gap between the wealthy and the poor, improving health, education and well-being of population, raising standards of national environment, diminishing the state interference with economy with an active role thereof and strengthening its institutional capacities. 
1.3.1. Strategy “Kazakhstan 2030” and the medium term development agenda.
The Government embarked on an intensive strategic planning process to set a vision and targets about the future of the new nation. This was reflected in the development of the long-term National Strategy ‘Kazakhstan 2030’. Being formally launched by the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan in October 1997 and addressing the top government leaders, parliamentarians, judiciary and academic circles, this document identifies seven strategic priorities where the development efforts are to be concentrated in the long-term perspectives. 
National security; 
Domestic political stability and consolidation of society;
Economic growth, based on a developed, market-oriented economy;
Health, education and well-being of the citizens of Kazakhstan;
Effective use of energy resources;
Development of modern infrastructure; and  
A professional state. 
Based on an integrated approach with respect to issues of sustainable development and in complement with the Strategy – 2030, the three-year programmes to underpin the long-term strategic priority directions have been developed. The 2000-2002 agenda, in particular, was presented in the November 1999 Report of the Prime Minister to the Parliament on the National Programme of Action. Macro- and micro-economic policies, tax and budget, agro-industrial, social, fiscal and credit, as well as regional policies were determined there as the key elements of the mid-term social and economic development of the country. Regarding the most critical social and economic problems, the government priorities include provision of social benefits, poverty eradication and employment generation, solution of the problem of internal debts, reforming healthcare system, provision of heating and electricity to household and fighting organised crime, corruption and drug abuse. 
On State Programme of Poverty Alleviation and Unemployment Control
Building on one of the core components of the National Programme of Action for 2000-2002, the State Programme of Poverty Alleviation and Unemployment Control is being elaborated by the leading specialists from more than 12 governmental bodies. Headed by the Deputy Prime Minister, the Ministry of Economy, Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, Ministry of Finance, the Commission on Family and Women’s Affairs and others involved parties has joint together to complete the draft Programme by March and to prepare a detailed action plan. The specific poverty eradication targets are being identified there through productive employment creation in the real sector of the economy, activation of small entrepreneurship, development of the system of micro-crediting, stage-by stage clearing of internal debts, increasing the minimum pension and further development of pension reform, strengthening the social safety net and other relevant sections. The State Programme will be submitted to the President in April 2000 and is expected to be adopted in 2nd quarter of 2000.
National Environment Action Plan
The definition of priorities for ecological policies and the development of mechanisms for their practical implementation, have become the main objectives of the National Environment Action Plan (NEAP). Implementation of environmental policy requires the compliance of the legal and regulatory framework, economic instruments and institutional provisions with the objectives of this policy, as well as timely consideration and evaluation of the social consequences of its implementation. The most important prerequisites for successful implementation of the National Action Plan are as follows:
economically sound system for environmental protection and use of natural resources;
optimal management structure for environmental protection;
stable financing mechanism for nature protection programs;
continuous environmental education and training;
participation of communities in decision making processes and supervision of environmental protection activities.  
National Healthcare Reform Programme
The National Healthcare Reform Programme has been one of the mid-term sectoral strategies developed within the framework of the long-term national strategy ‘Kazakhstan 2030’. It was officially launched in November 1998 and set the general directions for health reform. The reform aims at removing the government monopoly on health care, a shift from curative services towards preventive medicine, a higher priority for primary care, change of physicians specialisation from traditional grouping to the family physicians coupled with the switch from the visit to capitation payment system. The Health Programme envisages the steps that may serve potent enabling factors for the present programme implementation. They include a shift towards greater community participation, ensuring that decentralisation becomes dominant in the health systems that evolve, promoting multi-sectoral collaboration as a higher priority for the health ministry with better defining the roles of other ministries and NGOs.
National Healthy Lifestyle Development Strategy 
Having formally launched the Strategy 2030, the President addressed the Government with a set of most urgent and important tasks focused on meeting social and human needs of people. Importantly, one of tasks has been the promotion of nation-wide effort to develop healthy lifestyle. With strong co-ordination and technical support from the UN and the health donor group the Government responded with the formulation of the National Healthy Lifestyle Development Strategy during January-June 1998. Three levels of working groups were established, comprising of leading specialists from Government and technical experts from the health donor group, to proceeded with the planning along: (1) issue-specific components including nutrition, safe sex behaviour, alcohol/tobacco, communicable diseases, physical exercises, (2) methodological approaches such as information, education and communication (IEC), curricula development, development/revision of legislation, applied health research, and (3) the line of overall management and co-ordination. The draft National Healthy Lifestyle Development Programme was presented to the Government and donor community at the end June 1998 and shortly after was formally endorsed.
Program of Democratisation and Political Reform
On 30 September 1998 in his annual message to the people of Kazakhstan the President of the Republic proposed the Program of Democratisation and Political Reform. The following seven elements were announced as fundamental for the process of democratisation and political liberalisation: a) a representative and participatory electoral process; b) multiple national political parties; c) increased role of the National Parliament as a separate branch of power; d) strengthened role of non-government organisations in building civil society; e) a professionally functioning and autonomous judicial system; f) free, uncensored and independent press; g) increased status of women. The Program implementation pursues simplification of election law and procedures, creation of system for political parties training, provision of regular system of accountability of the Prime Minister and his Cabinet to the Parliament, simplification of registration and supervision procedures for domestic and international non-governmental organisations, enforcement of the Anti-Corruption Law, removal of any remaining impediments to a free press and strengthening of the role of the existing National Commission on Family and Women Affairs. 
National Action Plan on Improving the Status of Women
The National Commission on Family and Women Affairs under the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan was established in December 1998. Initiating a dialogue between all sections of society including government agencies, women’s NGOs and international organisations, the National Commission has co-ordinated the work of a thematic task force, which has resulted in the development and publication of the first National Action Plan on Improvement of Women’s Status in Kazakhstan (NAP). The NAP includes 12 critical areas of concern (Women and Poverty; Education and Training of Women; Women and Health; Violence against Women; Women and Armed Conflicts; Women and the Economy; Women in Power; Institutional Mechanisms for the Advancement of Women; Women’s Human Rights; Women and Mass Media; Women and the Environment; Girls). The existence of such programmes is in itself a good indication of the serious intention of the state to facilitate sustainable human development. At the same time, the NAP funding for implementation is envisaged mainly from sectoral and local budgets. Therefore, although international sources of a technical assistance nature are also enlisted in the NAP, the clear identification and full mobilisation of financial resources is a matter of utmost importance for the success of the Action Plan. 
1.3.2	UN Global Agenda: Implementation and Follow-up.
Since 1990, the international community has convened 12 major conferences on the main dimensions of economic and social development. Taken together, these high profile meetings have committed Governments to address the most pressing problems facing today’s world, to re-think their development policies and development co-operation. Nevertheless, due to the diversity in political, social and economic levels of development the Kazakhstan responses to global commitments and programmes of action also vary. Kazakhstan having ratified various international conventions has until recently reported only on the Convention on Biodiversity. A major challenge for the government of the republic and the UN system is therefore to facilitate and to meet these obligations. Recent indications seem to suggest that the government is now moving in this direction on environment and education, women, labour, climate change and human rights (see Table 1.2. for selective summary).
Thus, the report on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women was prepared and presented by the task force in October 1999. The multi-agency task force with the Government and non-governmental representation addressed the UN Country Team for the expert support to the report formulation process. Responding to this request the UNDP Regional Bureau in co-operation with its Swedish partners have provided series of training for the task force members on the UN reporting requirements. In April 2000, the Government of Kazakhstan will report to the UN on the status of implementation of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or degrading Treatment or Punishment (CAT). The report on the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) would be prepared by mid-2000. The United Nations Country Team, and UNICEF in particular, would assist the Government both in preparation of the report and its presentation to the UN Executive Board. 
Following four national meetings and a regional conference in Almaty in November 1999 carried out with lead support from UNDP, a stronger awareness and consensus for action has been developed. The National Commission on Human Rights is currently negotiating with the Government on ratification of the International Convenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (CESCR), the International Convenant on Civil and Political Rights (CCPR), as well as the Optional Protocols (OPT and OPT2) to the CCPR.

Part 2.	Implications of the Development Assistance for the United Nations system cooperation
2.1	Overview of the Development Assistance to the Country in 1992 - 1999 
Kazakhstan started receiving external assistance in 1992 immediately following independence in December 1991, for the purpose of changing the course of development towards a market-based economy and democratic society. In this period, the economic crises made it impossible for Kazakhstan to generate sufficient resources to launch economic reforms. Requiring broad financial and technical assistance, the Government was open to the transformation strategies proposed and even initiated by the donors. 
Most of the ODA at that time was devoted to budget and balance of payments, support of economic reforms, financial management and banking, and institutional capacity building. Thus, the IBRD Rehabilitation Loan (USD180 million) and Structural Adjustment Loan (SAL, USD180 million) were aimed at reforms in privatisation and the financial sector. IMF disbursed some USD 460 million between 1993-1995 to assist the Government in reducing inflation ADB approved its first loan of USD60 million financing critically needed imports and public and private enterprises. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) signed its first loan on SME Development Programme (USD122 million).
By 1995 and 1996 a number of new multilateral and bilateral donors appeared in Kazakhstan (Islamic Development Bank (IDB), Canada, Kuwait and others). Gradually increasing the volume of assistance with every year, major donors in co-operation with the Government had developed country programmes focused on specific areas in accordance with their mandates and experience. The Government had clarified its immediate priorities and was in the process of mid- and long-term development planning. 
In October 1997 the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan announced the country's long-term development strategy (Kazakhstan 2030) which became a policy framework for the mid-term sectoral and regional programmes. By 2000-2002 it is planned to finish structural reforms, increase the private sector’s share in GDP, keep a controlled budget deficit and support stability of the national currency rate. The purpose of the social policy in this period is to stop the decline in the standards of living and increase the volume and quality of social services. The Government's interest to receive the development assistance in line with the national priorities became much stronger than it had been in the early stages of co-operation. Therefore, some of the previously planned donor projects were cancelled, and new activities occurred in accordance with current development needs.
In 1998 multilateral assistance represented more than 80%of the total external disbursements (USD490.1 million). IMF and IBRD had the largest share with USD217 million and USD 210 million respectively, followed by ADB, EBRD and EU. Bilateral donor provided USD109 million of assistance to Kazakhstan, of which the largest were from USA, Japan, and Saudi Arabia. The year 1998 also saw an increase in the United Nations grant assistance up to USD6.9 million, although in 1999 due to decline of grant funds and some co-financing its total amount decreased by 20%. Thus, funds released from UNDP (USD1.9 million) decreased by 31% compared to 1998, disbursements from UNICEF (USD1.4 million) and UNFPA (USD 0.7 million) decreased by 22% and 34% respectively. 
However, overall UN funds remain about the same proportion (rank) as in 1998. Some agencies, including UNESCO, UNHCR, and UNAIDS have even increased their assistance to Kazakhstan. The Bretton Woods Institutions were again the leaders in loan funds along with EBRD, Japan and ADB. The World Bank has approved the Road Transport Rehabilitation Project (USD100 million), Health project (USD42.5 million), Legal Reform (USD16.5 million) and Electricity Transmission Rehabilitation (USD 140 million) projects. The IMF made a commitment USD453 million under a three-year extended fund facility in support of the Government and the National Bank’s economic reform programme.

The overall picture of the United Nations presence in Kazakhstan shows that the UN development assistance is not concentrated in particular region, but broadly disseminated throughout the whole territory of the republic (see Map 2.1 below). One of the largest recipients of the UN assistance among administrative territories is the city of Almaty, the former capital of the country. A developed network of business, educational and cultural institutions, a large number of civil society organisations predetermined a considerable share of projects being implemented in Almaty. Although, due to transfer of the capital, the UN country team, in order to continue its co-operation with the government, had opened a liaison office in Astana and moved some of the projects to the new capital. 
Another large portion of UN rehabilitation, recovery and sustainable human development projects are located in Semipalatinsk. Pursuant to the UN General Assembly Resolution (52/169M) which called for international assistance to those affected by the history of Semipalatinsk Test Site, UNESCO, UNICEF, WHO, UNFPA, UNV, UNDP, ILO and other UN offices started and extended their presence in this area. The next three administrative territories who benefit from the UN development assistance are South-Kazakhstan (Shymkent), Kyzylorda (Aral Sea), and Karaganda (Temirtau) oblasts. 2.2.	Lessons Learned from UN Development Assistance.
During the last few years since the establishment of its presence in Kazakhstan, the UN system made a major impact on priority development problems in the republic. Implementation of the 'Global Agendas' has improved significantly through the strengthened processes and mechanisms and achievements toward fulfilling international goals and targets. Collaboration within the UN system, as well as with the government, civil society and the donor community, enhanced the impact of the UN development system and contributed to better utilisation of each agency’s capacities and resources. 
The analysis of accomplishments achieved by the UN Country Team in Kazakhstan has demonstrated that the effective collaboration, coupled with success of individual agencies, were facilitated by the mutual agreement about priority needs, programme co-operation, effective information sharing and growing recognition of the UN system as a reliable development partner. Nevertheless, a few problems and challenges are still remaining. The effectiveness of the team to achieve its goals was constrained for the following main reasons: 
frequent government restructuring, significant down-sizing and turnover within the framework of public administration, democratic and other transition reforms; 
the move of the capital to Astana followed by a certain time for settling in and new organisational arrangements within the relevant government counterparts; 
limited human and financial resources are limited. 
The above factors had a certain negative influence on UN programme activities and planned events, although the country team made a significant effort to overcome difficulties. Some of the constraints have been partly offset by significant improvements in cost sharing and establishment of a liaison UN office in the new capital city Astana. To go further in this direction, the UN/Government Retreat on formulation of the UN Development Assistance Framework, which was held in Almaty on 28-29 May 1999, have identified the following lessons learned from UN development assistance:
for the purpose of awareness raising and recognition, the ideas and recommendations provided by the UN agencies and organisations should have clear ownership;
to avoid false expectations, the UN agencies’ programmes should be realistic and coincide with national development priorities and correct needs assessment;
more attention should be given to monitoring and evaluation of programmed activities to properly assess the progress, consolidate the achievements and follow up;
to avoid overlapping and inefficient use of resources the UN agencies’ programmes should be well coordinated within the UN and donor community. 
Based on the identified lessons and to timely and most effectively adjust to changing economic, social and political situation in Kazakhstan the agencies agreed that there is a need for more regular exchange of information on current situation analysis and implications for the future. The agencies have also agreed to look more systematically at global agenda and international conventions to make concerted efforts to follow-up. 
To simplify rules and procedures on the programming level and thus to enhance the UN collaboration in the field level, the Country Team agencies have now harmonised their programming cycles. UNDP, UNICEF and UNFPA, as well as several other agencies, including UNESCO, ILO, UNAIDS, UNIDO and the World Bank have synchronised their next programmes to start in 2000. In the future, to avoid unnecessary difficulties in joint programming the agencies agreed to negotiate with their respective headquarters on flexibility to adjust the duration of individual programme cycles.

3.1	Preparation of the UNDAF.
3.1.1.	The UNDAF Process and Participation
The preparation of a Common Country Assessment (CCA) in Kazakhstan as a first stage in developing the UNDAF was in line with ongoing efforts to enhance collaboration and integration of UN system activities in the country. The CCA process was launched by consultations, inviting and assembling substantial contributions from all UN agencies, other donors and the government. At the regular and special inter-agency meetings the CCA drafts were discussed and commented on. Through continuous consultations at various levels and integration of inputs, the CCA was finalised and widely circulated in early 1999. 
The Country Strategy Note (CSN), which has been earlier planned as a strategic agenda for joint programming in complement to the CCA, was difficult for the Country Team to launch in 1997 and early 1998.  Repeated government restructuring, downsizing and fragmentation of aid co-ordination and management institutions, as well as UN staff turnover and disparate programme cycles significantly hampered the efforts to formulate CSN. The UNDAF, which seeks to bring together the policy planning and actions of the UN Funds and Programmes, was reconsidered by the Country Team as feasible and preferable to the CSN. The good experience of pilot countries also contributed to the decision to formulate an UNDAF with effect from 2000. 
The UNDAF is based on the CCA, national strategies and plans, individual Country Programmes and other programme and evaluation documents. Its formulation benefited from the full collaboration of all UN organisations, agencies and Bretton Woods Institutions represented in Kazakhstan. All resident offices, as well as some regional offices and non-resident organisations, participated as equal members in the process through thematic groups’ consultations and regular Heads of Agency meetings, which were used as a vehicle to consolidate all substantive inputs. 
The first draft was reviewed and the common programme framework for the next 5-year period was refined during the UN/Government Inter-Agency Retreat held outside Almaty on 28-29 May, 1999 and resulted in agreement about needs and opportunities for UN development co-operation and identified specific approaches for programme synergy. Members of the UN Country Team, having participated in laying the foundations for inter-agency collaboration at the concrete project implementation levels, demonstrated a commitment to follow up.
Several ministers and vice-ministers, as well as other senior government officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Health, Education and Sports, Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment Protection, National Commission on Family and Women Affairs, Agency for Strategic Planning and Agency for Economic Planning participated actively in the assessments and conclusions. Discussions focused on how the Country Team would follow-up to global and national development agenda, strengthen thematic areas of cooperation and joint programming, and improve aid coordination with Government and other donors. 
Draft revisions of the UNDAF have been sent at three stages to non-resident agencies to ensure their involvement both in the UNDAF preparation and its further implementation processes. Working groups with distributed leadership and shared responsibilities have tackled the themes of greatest interest and challenge for collaboration. 
3.1.2.	Lessons Learned during UNDAF Preparation
The process of the UNDAF formulation besides exercising the participatory approach was a useful exercise itself in terms of revealing the problem areas and advantages of the existing Resident Co-ordinator’s system and UN country team co-operation and capacities. 
Improved information exchange opens up broader chances for collaboration. As was mutually agreed by the UN country team members, the existing system of the regular inter-agency meetings does not sufficiently facilitate the agencies to learn enough information  about each other’s activities and to identify the feasible opportunities for practical cooperatuion. In complement to non-harmonised programme cycles and other objective factors, this lack of information in its turn has also negatively influenced the willingness of the agencies to collaborate closer. More consultations at all level, informal and in meetings with other donors, or with Government, remain contributors of success. The participatory approach employed recently to finalise the UNDAF has greatly enhanced inter-agency information exchange. The new Common Premises will certainly increase information exchange and steps to bring more agencies on the LAN or e-mail networks would also help. 
UN-specific theme groups have had mixed effect. Some work well at each stage of the programme cycle, others proved to be paper intentions and were dormant. Therefore adjustments need to be made periodically and pragmatically. Theme groups worked best when a practical collaborative initiative provided the “glue” for cohesion and the incentive for an agency’s leadership.
Headquarters support, expectations and instructions to Kazakhstan seem to vary. Sincerity of commitment can be questioned by other UN partners or the country office staff themselves to take the time, to make the effort, and to collaborate. Individual agency image, recognition and funding objectives need to be blended and enhanced through joint ventures, which are more successful. Thus, headquarters’ support in encouraging agencies to take a more active stand on these inter-agency activities would therefore be appreciated
Personal commitments made by the heads of agencies leads to a broader involvement of national and programme staff at all levels. Although the commitment from agencies to collaborate was not questionable, bottlenecks have been encountered in the Kazakhstan CCA and UNDAF formulation processes. Thus, the difficulty on agencies’ sides to appoint a focal point for the exercise has first considerably delayed the overall process until heads of agencies became personally involved in the process by leading a number of related activities. The same bottlenecks might be encountered in future UNDAF implementation should these problems recur. In this context, since the UNDAF preparation and follow-up require special commitments from the agencies, staff designation in this time consuming process and the framework initiatives should be reflected in individual programmes, work plans and budgets. 
Active involvement of government and other partners in the UNDAF formulation increases support for its implementation. The Government of Kazakhstan although having been through frequent administrative and structural changes, the recent move to a new capital and therefore significant staff turnover continues to ask for United Nations development assistance on a wide range of issues. A number of thematic groups established within the UN programme activities are working in close co-operation with the relevant government counterparts and other civil society organisations. Senior government officials participating in the thematic groups meetings as well as in the UNDAF inter-agency retreat have taken the lead role in the formulation, discussion and approval of the framework. This participatory process has provided a favourable ground for further support for the framework activities at the implementation stage. 
Action to collaborate and achieve better results through synergy do not depend on the CCA or UNDAF. Experience clearly has shown that excellent practical work can easily proceed while the talking and writing go on, or before it begins for the CCA, UNDAF, CSN, etc. However, the CCA and new UNDAF are expected to enhance the process and results. 
3.2	Development Assistance Framework
3.2.1 Principles and Goals of UN development co-operation
The UN Inter-Agency and Government consultations that shaped the UNDAF identified the following broad functional goals and operational principles for the UN system activities and emphasised the shift of its development assistance from strategic and action planning to their implementation:
Functional goals, in which the UN system can play potentially more effective roles by collaborating together:
Advocacy and awareness raising;
Policy dialogue with the government on strategy/action planning and legislation;
Assistance for capacity development;
Implementation support in national and global agenda’s follow up;
Co-ordination and facilitation of development assistance;
Resource mobilisation.
Operational principles, which will guide the overall UNDAF strategy and the actions of collaborative initiatives evolved later in 3.2.2: 
reinforce the common UN mandates, promote synergy, divide responsibilities appropriately and avoid duplication
achieve greater impact at lesser cost for each individual agency and collectively;
increase the effective linkage between UN agencies and with the government and other partner’s 
improve communication and trust among the UN organisations;
increase cost-sharing and rational use of resources;
respect individual organisation’s mandates, comparative advantages, yet find and optimise selective collective efforts; 
improve co-ordinated follow-up to UN conferences, conventions and declarations;
projects formulated and improved to be sustainable or achieve sustainable results;
actions requested by government and/or stakeholders, and receiving their participation, support and sustained ownership.
 3.2.2	 Priority Themes and Strategic Roles for UN Development Assistance
Identifying priority themes and achieving practical collaboration have marched forward, but at a very uneven rate. Fortunately, practical co-operation has been achieved, which begins to fulfil UN functional goals and adhere to the operational principles. Since 1995, the first year of its full programme operations in Kazakhstan, the United Nations has been actively collaborating in such areas of mutual concern, as social and humanitarian needs; economic stabilisation and policy advice; capacity building of new institutions, environmental protection and engines for growth and employment. The experience of UN development assistance in the republic has deepened the understanding of individual mandates and goals within each of the above themes. Building on the conclusions of regular inter-agency meetings and thematic groups consultations, as well as the extensive preparation and follow up to the Country Team’s participation in the Turin Workshop in November 1997, the UN system in Kazakhstan has steadily expanded its rolling assessment of needs and opportunities, and updated its strategies and activities. 
At the May 1999 joint UN/Government retreat, aimed to discuss needs and opportunities for UN development co-operation, specific approaches for programme synergy were identified. Consensus was reached on the common programme framework for the next 5-year period. Building on the lessons learned from previous UN development assistance, the areas for synergy and opportunities for inter-agency collaboration were then elaborated to further reflect the UN agencies’ programmes, strategies and plans. 
Four strategic priority areas were proposed as a focus for development cooperation supported by UN system in Kazakhstan. While these areas will form the basis of collaborative initiatives, the individual agencies will maintain identity and follow their mandate, but it will enhance clarity of responsibilities and ownership. 3.2.3 Strategic objectives
Development Challenge (1): Social Security and Human Development
Strategic Objective: To alleviate poverty, reduce human insecurity, raise income, and to reverse the growing gaps of wealth and living standards in pursuit of sustainable human development
Resulting from the economic downfall, the majority of the population has faced obvious deterioration in incomes and living standards and, and the availability and quality of basic services e.g. health and education has significantly decreased, especially in the rural areas. These insecurities and decreased services affect large part of the population and are especially manifested in several vulnerable groups, such as the unemployed, people with low-income, women, inhabitants of ecologically devastated regions, people affected by occupational hazards and the handicapped. Therefore, in the shorter term, the most urgent need is creating jobs and combating poverty and unemployment. Another priority area is to reverse the trend of decreasing quality and availability of social services for health and education. Health reform and preventive health offer excellent opportunities to achieve impact. Finalisation of social and economic reforms, primarily in the budgetary sphere leading to timely and complete payments of pensions, wages, salaries and social benefits is another key intervention needed. In the medium to longer term, the Government is expecting to achieve economic growth, and thus to ensure the equality of opportunities for all, a narrowed gap between the wealthy and the poor, improved health, education and welfare through steadfast settlement of social problems which arise in the course of the transition. 
The maximum impact and leverage for the UN development assistance can be achieved through both up- and downstream interventions such as facilitation of catalytic macro-policy interventions, capacity building and strengthening the effectiveness of relevant Government and civil society institutions in the areas of services provision, along with promotion of local communities self-reliance. As UN experience in Kazakhstan has shown, these steps are essential to ensure sustainability of the assistance. The UN system co-operation should therefore be focused on assisting the Government in the following areas: 
Poverty Alleviation, Employment, Social services and Social Safety. The UN system will assist the Government in the development of effective strategies and a coherent policy framework for income generation and SME development. Projects and advice will help  design and implement programmes to support employment promotion and income generation especially through development of micro and small enterprises, establishment of business advisory centres and micro-crediting in targeted oblasts and areas with the greatest poverty and income disparities. UNDP, UNV, ILO and UNIDO play key roles. In addition, UN support, including World Bank and ADB support to reform and improve effectiveness of social services is essential, but the government will need to give higher priority to these areas to halt the deterioration of the services and increase their quality. UNICEF, UNESCO, WHO, and UNFPA, as well as the WB will continue to have complementary programmes and some joint efforts. Special consideration should be given to vulnerable groups and women. 
(ii) Health and Healthy Lifestyles. The UN system will assist in implementation of national policies and programmes for promotion of healthy lifestyles with a main focus on the prevention of the further spread of HIV/AIDS, STD and drug abuse in Kazakhstan. Activities will include advocacy, policy dialogue, technical assistance for introduction of legislation for an effective response, clarification and commitment to policy and programme priorities, expansion of pilot projects and information-education-communication campaigns. Under the UN Theme Group, UNAIDS, UNESCO, UNFPA, UNICEF, WB, UNDP, UNODCCP and WHO will work jointly to address different targets, capacities and assist various sectors including health, education and justice/information.
In the field of women’s health, UNFPA, UNICEF, UNDP, UNAIDS, UNECSO and WHO will coordinate their efforts in strengthening capacity of an efficient network of quality reproductive health services, fully integrated in the reformed system of family doctors, with special attention to the sustainability of community based services through local NGOs and effective planning and monitoring system. Activities will also include increasing awareness and knowledge among young people, men and women with respect to reproductive rights and enhanced health related behaviour as promoted through the healthy lifestyles initiative. In order to operationalise streamlined policies regarding women’s health and gender issues, UN agencies will support the national health care reforms and integrated primary health care project models.
In order to decrease morbidity and mortality from common diseases among children under five, UNICEF and WHO will continue supporting Integrated Management of Childhood Illness and develop expansion models with government partners. Micronutrients deficiencies such as anaemia and IDD will be brought to high level attention to initiate necessary legislation on food fortification. UNICEF and WHO will also focus on the area of strengthening national capacity in procurement of EPI vaccines through National Regulatory Authority. WHO will also collaborate work with WB on tuberculosis. Special attention will be given to develop resource optimisation strategies and budget planning for social sectors including health by UNDP, UNFPA and WB.
UN support will also concentrate on geographically focused programmes in environmentally devastated areas of Aral Sea, Semipalatinsk and Caspian Sea, in the areas of above mentioned fields and in community based environmental health promotion activities within integrated programmes of income generation, environment restoration and community development.
 Education for All, Reforms, Training in Key Capacities. The Government has requested UN assistance in preparation of the national EFA Status Report for its presentation at the global EPA Conference in Senegal, April 2000 and in formulation of measures to weather the transition period through urgent, mid- and long-term interventions. A 2-phase approach will be carried out to tackle the present education situation in the country: 1) urgent measures to mitigate the impact of the socio-economic transition; 2) mid- and long-term measures to address education development. In the light of this, the strategic objectives to be considered are the following:
On point 1.   a) to mitigate the slowing down and decline of the overall education system, especially in the field of early childhood care and education; b) in the case of the basic education sub-sector, while enrolment rates, intake rates and overall participation remain high, this has been maintained at the expense of teacher salaries, sharp decline in the quality of education facilities, low level of learning outcomes and of instructional materials. This reflects efforts by parents and the Government alike to sustain the quantitative achievements of the system, but at the detriment of qualitative development.
On point 2.  a) there is a need for a serious revamping of the management of the overall education sector, and to articulate education goals and targets with those of national development plans such as “2030”; b) mid- and long term practices badly need to be introduced such as new management and financing techniques, decentralisation to the oblast education offices; establishment of a national EMIS (Education Management Information System) and training of mid-level managers; c) retraining of teachers on innovative  pedagogical instruments and techniques, proper to a market-geared economy are also needed.  
While the objective UNESCO partners in this endeavour remain mainly UNICEF, UNDP and development banks, there is a need for coordination at 2 levels: a) policy guidance, advice and formulation, including training of senior decision-makers, and b) at the grass-roots level, coordination in the implementation modalities jointly with civil society (communities), NGOs and PTAs (parent-teacher associations).       
In addition, informal education, information and communication is judged as a powerful cross-cutting theme of UN cooperation (with other donors). This affects every level of practice and policy: government and parliament, local institutions like NGOs and CBOs, population segments including women, labour, the poor and vulnerable, as well as personal behaviour and initiatives. The UN will sharpen its work with media, other institutions and target groups, both dividing UN responsibilities and concentrating on achieving goals such as improved human rights, population, economic rehabilitation and SMEs, water and environment protection and gender equality. 
Development Challenge (2): Economic Management and Effective Governance
Strategic Objective: To measurably strengthen performance and efficiency of people centred governance for sustainable local and national development
In accordance with the national development strategies and priorities, the UN will help the Government of Kazakhstan continue its course towards strengthening the transition reforms and achieving people-centred economic recovery and growth. Government policies although oriented towards a more limited role, need to be combined with an active and effective responsibility of the state. To achieve this overall objective the UN system (especially UNDP, WB, ILO, UNHCR, etc.) will help Government to develop a professional governance system based on efficient institutional co-ordination, decentralisation and increased accountability and responsibilities within administrative bodies, prevention and combating of corruption, and improvements in civil service systems. 
The UN system’s access to world-wide experience in reform and economic transition, as well as its neutrality and flexibility makes it well placed to be involved in sensitive up-stream areas of facilitating policy advice, high level strategic planning and implementation support and aid co-ordination. In the next 5-year period the UN system assistance to the Government would be focused on the following areas:
Strategic Planning and Policies, whereby the UN organisations would be instrumental in strengthening Government capacity to develop and implement long- and medium-term plans and to generate an on-going flow of key, strategic policy recommendations that address critical issues in Kazakhstan’s economic and social development and steer the growth and enhance human security of strategic sectors. 
 Public Sector Management and Government Practices, to strengthen the effectiveness of governance, will result in new or more effective Ombudspersons capacity of parliamentary structures, anti-corruption bodies, and other human rights promotion and oversight bodies. The Government is also expecting the UN system organisations to assist in implementation of the civil service reform initiatives, including merit-based selection and recruitment, resulting in a more efficient and accessible public sector. Reform of judicial and legal structures and related policy formulation will also be among the UN strategic priorities. UNDP will be leading in these activities, with the WB and others.
 Aid Co-ordination. UNDP and the WB will continue to help Government improve its aid co-ordination and management in order to help it mobilise and manage resources and create sustainable management system. Other UN system organisations shall also assist the Government to improve co-ordination capacities and to raise the impact of the external assistance flows in special sectors by ensuring a high level of communication and co-ordination in the preparation and implementation of donor programmes. 
Development Challenge (3): Democracy and Participation
Strategic Objective: To accelerate the transition to sustained democracy, political pluralism and participation.
The Program of Democratisation and Political Reform was launched formally in the 1998 annual message of the President to the people of Kazakhstan. A representative and participatory electoral process; multiple national political parties; increased role of the Parliament; strengthened role of non-government organisations; autonomous judicial system; independent press; and increased status of women were announced as fundamental elements for the process of democratisation and political liberalisation. UN system co-ordinated assistance will strengthen Government and non-government capacities in the Programme implementation, especially through UNDP, which was already providing leadership and practical initiatives to strengthen the transition to democracy: e.g. Parliament, human rights, women equality and WID. The UN system will focus its support in the following areas: 
Human Rights, whereby the UN assistance to the Government will primarily: a) strengthen the national human rights institutions and mechanisms, including for the fair and effective determination of refugee status, through building capacity, strong advocacy; b) develop the legal system in the country in the realm of human rights and refugee law on the basis of international principles, norms and standards; c) enable civil society and government institutions to monitor efficiently the human rights situation in Kazakhstan in terms of implementation of the national and international human rights standards; d) promote awareness of human rights among the public as well as civil servants; and e) forge partnership as an instrument of promoting and strengthening the Ombudsman and human rights institutions. UNDP, UNHCR, UNICEF, INESCO, ILO, DPI, UNFPA will play key roles. UNCHR will be a lead non-resident partner.
 Civil Society, NGOs and Political Pluralism to help build the institutional capacity of public, not-for profit, and governmental organisations to deliver services to socially vulnerable groups of the population; to establish or strengthen further the interaction and practical partnership among the governmental and the non-governmental sector for better local deliverance of services; and to promote networking with a view to develop an active civil society and alleviation of the conditions of the poor in the transition period. The UN collective efforts will be targeted at provision of expertise, advisory and technical services in the areas of: a) strategic planning for establishing the direction of the organisation and its mission; b) fund-raising; c) creating a marketing orientation of the non-profit organisation; d) public relations and mass media contacts; e) financial management; f) personnel management; and g) contacts with governmental structures and not-for-profit organisations. Special emphasis will be at the local level, where international and national UNVs are expected to make a major impact on mainstreaming the effective work of NGOs. The NGO Resource Centre, principally led by UNDP will continue to involve other UN, donor and international NGOs to make an increasing impact in the performance and sustainability of hundreds of NGOs.  
 Gender Equality and Improvement of Women’s Status, whereby the UN system would assist in implementation of the National Action Plan on Improving the Status of Women in the Republic of Kazakhstan. The NAP had been developed in a follow-up to the Beijing Platform for Action by the Government in close partnership with women’s NGOs and international organisations, under direct technical and financial assistance from UN agencies. The assistance will be mobilised around the four national priority needs in gender issues, namely: economic advancement of women, promotion of women’s health, eradication of violence against women and increasing building women’s political capacities. Activities will include advocacy, capacity-building of national counterparts, policy dialogue, technical assistance for the introduction of gender-disaggregated statistics and utilisation of gender-sensitive indicators in national planning/programming, introduction of legislation for an effective response, expansion of pilot projects and IEC campaigns. 
Under the coordination of UNIFEM, the UN Theme Group on Gender, including UNESCO, UNFPA, UNICEF, WB, UNDP, WHO, UNAIDS, UNV, UNHCR, and ILO will work jointly to address gender issues and assist various sectors including poverty alleviation and economic empowerment of women, political participation of women, eradication of violence against women, women’s health, girl-children and education through gender mainstreaming of the existing and perspective programmes of the UN agencies. As a result of the joint collaborative efforts by the UN Thematic Group on Gender, a common gender strategy would be finalised, structured around the implementation of the National Action Plan on Improving the Status of Women in the Republic of Kazakhstan (NAP). To operationalise the implementation of stipulated tasks the UN Thematic Group has jointly decided to establish a UN Gender in Development (GID) Bureau extending capacities of the former UNDP GID Bureau with a focus on co-ordinated technical and organisational capacity-building of key stakeholders and mobilising resources around NAP implementation.
Playing a catalytic role, the UN/Government initiative is already being reinforced by a joint commitment from other donor organisations, including OSCE, Canada Fund, USAID, USIS, British Council, British Know How Fund, Counterpart Consortium, Counterpart Humanitarian Assistance Programme, to provide continuous co-ordinated assistance in the NAP implementation in the Republic of Kazakhstan.
Development Challenge (4): Environment and Sustainable Development
Strategic Objective: To markedly impact environmentally sound and sustainable and development to overcome ecological, economic and social consequences of past disasters and current inappropriate practices and management.
Among the critical problems affecting the people and future sustainable growth are drying up of the Aral Sea and flooding of the Caspian Sea, shortage of safe drinking water, unsustainable agricultural practices, unsustainable exploitation of natural resources, insufficient use of energy, nuclear pollution, pollution from mining and other natural resources extraction industries, and human encroachment of ecological system. 
Government will establish its policies and priorities and improve its capacities in co-ordination to deal with these complex problems. Over the next 5 years, Government expects the UN system to be among the main development partners in the implementation of the National Environmental Action Plan, and the Biodiversity Strategy and Plan. In addition, assistance is expected especially from the WB, UNDP as well as UNICEF, UNESCO, FAO and IFAD to develop and implement a national Agenda 21, and a practical medium-term Water Security Programme. A broad participatory approach with UN help will make the process sustainable, including active involvement of local communities, NGOs, private sector, national and local government and other interested parties in programme and project formulation, and selective and effective utilisation of international experience. At the Government request the UN system will play a catalytic role to assist and facilitate co-ordination of other donor’s activities and to attract more funds from GEF, Montreal Protocol, Capacity 21, Trust Fund, other donors and investors. The UN is expected to focus its support on the following areas: 
By provision of general support to the Implementation of the National Environment Action Plan, the United Nations development system in Kazakhstan, especially WB and UNDP will assist the Government in formulating and implementing priority policies and programmes, and build requisite capacities, and to mobilise support. 
Protection, stabilisation, recovery and development of water based problems, whereby Government recognises the UN’s comparative advantage in assistance to stabilise the environment, to rehabilitate the disaster zones, to improve the management of the international waters, and to build the capacity of the regional institutions. The UN’s collective efforts with other donors will be targeted towards strengthening national policies, regulatory and institutional arrangements aimed at protection of biodiversity, support of mechanisms of co-ordination and co-operation, as well as harmonisation of environmental standards. The WB and UNDP will help Government (and stakeholders) formulate a Water Security Programme in 2000-2001, with grant and loan components, policy and advocacy dimensions, national and regional objectives and concrete targets. Other UN system partners will be selectively involved especially in regard to environment health. 
 Area-based environmental management programmes, to support actions for addressing the environmental problems in the most affected areas, and immediate rehabilitation measures at the local level.
