3.3	Implementation Arrangements
3.3.1 UN Inter-Agency Co-operation  
Following the Secretary-General's Programme for reforms, which emphasises the need for the UN system to act as a more co-ordinated organisation, the Kazakhstan UNDAF gives attention, first of all and as much as feasible to programme co-operation itself and to the implementation tools and instruments, as well as sharing of premises and services as key elements for the UN Country Team building. 
Relationship with the Bretton Woods Institutions
Since establishment in Kazakhstan the BWI and UN system organisations have identified common interests as reported in Annual reports of the Resident Co-ordinator. Co-operation is very good, with the World Bank and IMF [participating in the CCA and UNDAF, and some theme groups with UN and donors. The major focus has been on urgent social and humanitarian needs, economic stabilisation, critical policy advice and capacity building. As the experience of the BWI/UN has shown here in Kazakhstan, a strategic partnership between development entities is most required when the global agenda is to be further implemented and successfully followed-up, particularly with respect to growing emphasis by the UN and all specialised agencies on poverty eradication. The BWI/UN collaboration in Kazakhstan takes a variety of forms, including facilitating dialogue with government officials, other donors, and civil society, providing technical assistance linking grants and loans, preparing complementary needs assessment, and mutually reinforcing policies and strategies. 
Dimensions of on-going co-operation and future partnership between the BWI and UN agencies are already reflected above and include: a) public sector management, legal reform and government practices; b) poverty eradication, social protection, health and healthy life styles; c) water, environmental protection with co-ordination in the Aral Sea and Caspian programmes; d) information, education and communication; e) agriculture; f) SMEs and private sector development. WHO helps to implement part of one on-going WB loan. This could be a model for other loans during the coming years for which the UN organisations could provide management support and implementation services to speed and ensure synergy and efficiency of loan execution. 
Common Premises
Excellent results were achieved in Kazakhstan with regards to sharing of premises and services among UN agencies. In 1998, the Government offered the new rent-free offices in the cities of Almaty and Astana (the present capital city). Although being through stage-by-stage renovation a new Almaty office was jointly opened and is now well functioning and shared by UNAIDS, UNHCR, UNIDO, ILO, UNESCO, UNFPA, UNSD, UNV, DPI, WHO, UNDP and OSCE. All these agencies to a larger or smaller extent also share common services, such as conference room facilities, utilities, reception, telephones, travel services, customs clearance, building management and transport. The majority of agencies share the full range of administrative services including contracting, payments, accounting etc. 
A new dimension of UN collaboration in this area has been introduced with the Government's official move to Astana. In 1998 the day the new capital was inaugurated, a UN/UNDP liaison function was established there. Initially given a mandate to assist UN agencies with logistical arrangements, towards the end of 1998 this function’s capacity was expanded into being able to give support for programme activities. Joint premises in Astana are currently shared by the agencies either on a residential, or a visiting basis. Since the transition period is expected to continue for a few years, the presence in both cities is expected for some time.
Regular Interagency Meetings
The Resident Co-ordinator System has been effective not only in periodic exchange of information, problem-solving, administrative management issues, and common system strategies and concerns. Regular meetings have confirmed to be a catalytic vehicle for identifying opportunities for collaboration, working out practical programme and project co-operation, and monitoring progress and building greater coherence and linkages. Thematic groups periodically meet based on needs. Taking a pragmatic, opportunistic and catalytic approach these most often involve interested UN agencies working as well as other donors.  This applies especially to the health group, the SME (micro-credit group), the environmental group, the women/gender group, and the NGO group. Special groups also focus on the three geographic areas where the UN and Donors respond to special ecological-economic-social issues: Semipalatinsk, Aral Sea and Caspian region. This meeting can also play the role of a forum for joint programme implementation, monitoring and evaluation. 
UN Thematic and Working Groups
Thematic groups among agencies have been formed and reconfigured periodically to reflect national priorities and the evolving interest and opportunities for UN system co-operation. It should be noted that many theme groups meet with other donors in response to practical interests to co-ordinate. In our experience, some UN Theme groups are highly desirable and effective; others it is best to implement with other interested donors or stakeholders. UN Thematic Groups reflect the need for co-ordination in the following thematic areas:
Poverty Alleviation, Employment, Social Safety: UNDP, WB UNICEF, WHO, ODCCP, UNFPA, UNESCO, UNV, UNIDO, ILO, UNHCR. 
HIV/AIDS, Vulnerable Groups, Drugs: UNDP, WB, UNICEF, WHO, ODCCP, UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNESCO, UNV. 
Gender Mainstreaming: UNDP, UNICEF, WHO, UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNESCO, UNHCR.
Environment & Sustainable Development: UNDP, UNV, UNIDO, and WB.
In co-operation with above there are groups that encompass bilateral and multilateral donors: 
The Integrated Health Group, which has built upon steady and systematic co-operation between agencies and donors since 1995 and have now attracted close to 10 donors to push forward the integrated programme to address overall health needs of Kazakhstan. 
The SME Group and Micro-Lending Group have been active in Semipalatinsk. The successful implementation will serve as an example to replicate in the Caspian Sea region.
Aral Sea Group, which was created as a follow-up to special decision between the Government representatives, SG and UN Agency Heads to develop and implement a special 3-year programme on Aral Sea Rehabilitation, designed in 1997. 
Donor Group on Semipalatinsk, which was established in response to General Assembly Resolution A/51/L.61 to assist the Government to implement a special Semipalatinsk Relief and Rehabilitation Programme and follow-up to the goals of the Tokyo Global Conference.
3.3.2	Monitoring and Evaluation
To facilitate the implementation of the UNDAF, the Country team plans to carry out its annual, mid-term and final monitoring and evaluation with membership from each UN country team agency, relevant Government institutions, and as appropriate NGOs, and donors. The Government is expected to co-chair annual reviews of progress towards UNDAF objectives. The theme groups will also act as an area specific point of contact and initiator of joint implementation, monitoring, review and evaluation. Benchmarks and related success indicators need to be further developed and used based on expected impact and current situation for each collaborative programme theme. Monthly Inter-Agency meetings and annual Resident Co-ordinator’s Reports will also continue to be used as reporting instruments for progress against the UNDAF implementation.

Annex 1.	Operational Programmes and Activities of United Nations Organisations and Agencies 
The United Nations system in Kazakhstan is currently represented by 15 organisations: UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, UNODCCP, UNHCR, UNV, UNIFEM, ILO, UNESCO, WHO, UNIDO, WB, IMF, UNAIDS and UN/DPI. Actively collaborating with the Government, non-governmental organisations and donor partners UN-family agencies go through the annual process of evaluation of their activities and the achieved results. The challenge for the nearest future would be to meet priorities beyond the year 2000 and start the new century and the millennium with new development perspectives.
Since establishment in 1993, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Kazakhstan has been harmonising its programme and project activities with the national strategic objectives, focusing on social development and poverty alleviation; effective governance within a democratic framework; equitable economic growth; and sustainable management of the environment. UNDP consultants successfully helped the government to formulate the national privatisation program. Advisory services were also provided to formulate and implement the National Environmental Action Plan for Sustainable Development, National Action Plan on Improvement of Status of Women, Social Development Promotion Initiative (SDPI), Healthy Lifestyle Promotion programme, and other action plans. Another priority task has been to improve governance of institutions. UNDP was among the lead donors who reacted to the 40-year nuclear tradegy in Semipalatinsk with comprehensive Relief and Rehabilitation programme. With UNDP help, Kazakhstan has joined several UN instruments on Human Rights protection and has strengthened other democratic institutions, including NGOs, Parliament. UNDP’s total grant financing grew up to US$ 10 million since 1993, an increasingly large share of which (from 20% in 1997 to 48% in 1999) came from cost-sharing. 
The Program of Co-operation in 1995-1999 between the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), and the Government of Kazakhstan, consisted of five areas: Child and maternal health; Child and maternal nutrition; Basic education; Water supply and sanitation, and Planning and advocacy. The main thrust in the programme was on mother and child health and nutrition. Kazakhstan managed with UNICEF support to reverse the increasing trend in child mortality, and child mortality has been falling the last years. Ratification by Kazakhstan of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) gave UNICEF a stronger advocacy platform for child rights. The UNICEF program in Kazakhstan also included support to the Aral Sea Program for Environment and Regional Assistance (ASPERA), by provision of vaccines, syringes, basic drugs and equipment for primary health care, provision of basic education supplies for classrooms, training of teachers, provision of safe drinking water for schools, improvement of sanitation facilities in schools. Agreement on a programme of co-operation for the years 2000 –2004 was signed between the Government and UNICEF in February 2000.The programme is based on a child rights approach, targeting health as before, but with more weight on education, and with support to children in need of special protection, juvenile justice and young peoples participation as new elements. 
The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) assistance to Kazakhstan began in 1992 and since then has been mainly provided toward improvement of Reproductive Health/Family Planning Services and IEC Support to Reproductive Health. During 1993-1996 a wide variety of medical equipment for maternal health and family planning have been supplied by UNFPA (USD 1,6 million). In 1996, the Government of Kazakhstan endorsed three major UNFPA projects in the areas of reproductive health and family planning resulted in equipment supply, establishment of training centres and the training for service providers, dissemination of information among population on modern methods of family planning through local NGOs. In 1998-1999 in response to the Government's Social Strategic Plan by the year 2030, UNFPA assisted the Government in formulation of population policy and provided support to Kazakhstan’s first Census. Recently the UNFPA Country Programme for Kazakhstan for the years 2000-2004 was approved aimed to provide $ 6.0 million of grant funds. 
The United Nations Office on Drug Control and Crime Prevention (ODCCP) implements one national and one regional projects in Kazakhstan. In July 1997 the Project “Institutional Building and Drug Control Measures Improvement in Kazakhstan”  (USD774 thousands) started to support the Government in drug control measures through providing consultative assistance, training of drug control bodies. Another project “Mapping of the territories with drug contained plants in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tadjikistan” (USD742 thousands) started in December 1997. At the request of President of the republic of Kazakhstan ODCCP assisted Government to prepare in 1998, its medium-term programme (Masterplan) to combat drugs and criminality, total budget will be about USD 5,5 millions. New national and regional projects are anticipated to deal better with demand/supply reduction and trafficking of drugs taking account of the growing challenges and recent best practices. 
The Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) was opened in September of 1995 in order to support the Government and non-governmental entities to strengthen the legal basis and institutional structures for coping with refugees and refugee related issue. There is an estimate of 14,500 refugees currently living in Kazakhstan, mainly from Tajikisatn, Afghanistan and Chechnya. The Liaison Office in Almaty has been implementing a number of projects aiming at the protection and assistance of refugees as well as at the promotion of refugee law. These projects allowed for a certain progress in the country’s capacity to deal with refugees, documented in the accession of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees in January of 1999; creation of a governmental procedures for refugee status determination; as well as the drafting of a national Refugee Law to be submitted to Parliament during 2000. Additionally, UNHCR has been conducting a series of seminars and workshops on international refugee instruments and has co-published a number of documents relating to human rights and refugees. Material assistance is being provided by UNHCR to the most vulnerable groups among the refugee population though the Kazakhstan Red Crescent and Red Cross Society. As a long-term strategy, UNHCR Almaty has made an effort to promote the capacity of Kazakhstan to handle potential refugee influxes in an independent manner by providing technical expertise as well as general agency support to governmental and numerous non-governmental entities. In line with UNHCR’s general effort to support the development of a strong civil society, a number of national as well as refugee organisations, including the Kazakhstan Red Crescent and Red Cross Society, the Children’s Fund of Kazakhstan, and the International Bureau for Human Rights and the Rule of Law have as UNHCR’s implementing partners received substantial material support and training in topics concerning human rights and refugee law, organisational management, fincial accounting procedures, etc.  
The United Nations Volunteers (UNV) started its activities in Kazakhstan through the UNDP offices in 1995. Since then 50 volunteer specialists have worked on various projects, with the majority of them involved in the Programme of Rehabilitation and Capacity Building for the Aral Sea Region: to help improve the environment, raise the capacities of NGOs, and create employment. By the end of 1999 the UNV Programme was involved in at least 10 projects at 7 different locations in Kazakhstan, spanning specialities from HIV/AIDS prevention and computer programming to water resource management. An innovation that was introduced in January 1999 is the recruitment of national volunteer specialists, adding greater potential for long term sustainability through a mixed team capacity building approach. To date 10 local UNVs have been fielded with a further 10 in various stages of recruitment.
United Nations Development Fund for Women (UNIFEM) provides financial support and technical assistance to innovative programmes promoting women’s human rights, their economic and political empowerment, and gender equality. UNIFEM focuses its work at the country level in supporting the Resident Coordinator system in promoting gender mainstreaming within country programmes. In Kazakhstan since opening in July 1999 the UNIFEM has been implementing the UNDP, UNDGO and UNIFEM joint project “Support to the UN Resident Coordinator System on Implementing of Beijing Platform for Action”. The main objectives of this project are to support and assist in strengthening the UN system capacity to promote women’s empowerment and gender mainstreaming; support formulation and implementation of gender sensitive policies and programmes; to facilitate working relationships between UN agencies, civil society, and government to coordinate planning and implementation of Beijing Platform for Action follow-up strategies; contribute to the engendering of UN planning documents, such as the UNDAF, CCA and CCF, and facilitate UNIFEM activities in the areas of advocacy and building. 
Kazakhstan joined the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe  (UN/ECE) in 1994 and started practical participation in ECE activities in 1995. Technical assistance was provided to Kazakhstan mainly through the ECE Regional Advisory Services programme. During 1998, ECE rendered technical assistance to Kazakhstan in the fields of the energy, environment protection, and entrepreneurship and small and medium sized enterprises, transport infrastructure and border crossing facilitation, and statistics. Technical assistance was also provided by ECE and ESCAP in the preparation of the UN Special Programme for the Economies of Central Asia (SPECA). In the coming years, ECE and ESCAP are expected to assist Kazakhstan as the lead country to implement a SPECA project on transport infrastructure and border crossing facilitation. Kazakhstan will also benefit from other SPECA projects, namely: rational and efficient use of energy and water resources of Central Asia; international economic conference; regional co-operation in developing a multi-choice approach to hydrocarbon supply routes through pipelines to the world markets; and industrial restructuring with a view to creating internationally competitive manufacturing industries. 
The principal technical assistance to the Government provided by the International Labour Organisation (ILO) is channelled through two major projects: “Local economy restructuring and employment adjustment: Demonstration project for employment creation in depressed areas”(USD239 thousands) and “Start and improve your business”(USD250 thousands). Since establishment in 1995 ILO has provided various advisory services on determination of wages policy, elaboration of employment policy, etc. A number of workshops re1ated to occupational safety and health issues, as well to development and strengthening the tripartism system and tripartite relations, were held in Kazakhstan. ILO offered comments and recommendations to various drafts of Labour Law, Employment and Occupational Safety Insurance Laws of Kazakhstan. In 1995-1999 the ILO under the auspices of UNDP undertook an exploratory mission on Social Development Strategy, launched a survey “Enterprise restructuring in Kazakhstan”, assisted Kazakhstan to ratify several ILO Conventions on occupational safety and health, on the working environment and employment policy.  
Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nation (FAO) has not yet established its presence in Kazakhstan. During a needs assessment mission in May 1999, the following priority areas were identified in consultations with the Government for future cooperation between the Organisation and the Republic of Kazakhstan:
Capacity building to support the accession of Kazakhstan to the WTO.
Environment and AgroBioDiversity: follow-up action for each item was identified. 
Strategic framework for the development of the grains and livestock sub-sectors.
A strategic framework for poverty alleviation and food security in Kazakhstan.
Improving marketing services and market information network.
Pilot implementation of a micro lending scheme.
Within the "four potential priority and synergy areas" indicated in the UNDAF, the Organisation plans to contribute in the area of "Environment and Sustainable Development". In particular, FAO has a long experience and the relevant expertise in water resources management and policies and other related issues. It has organised and led the sub-regional Expert Consultation on Water Policy reform in Central Asia, held in Kazakhstan in July 1999. FAO's expertise also allows contributing to the area of "Economic Management and Effective Governance", as well as "Social Security and Human Development" as this also relates to the macro and sectoral management of the agriculture sector and food security.
The mandate of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) is to contribute to peace and security in the world by promoting collaboration among nations through education, science, culture and communication in order to further universal respect for justice, for the rule of law and the human rights and fundamental freedoms which are affirmed for the peoples of the world, without distinction of race, sex, language or religion, by the Charter of the United Nations. The UNESCO office in Almaty was established in 1994 and since then has played a leading role in coordinating donor assistance in the sphere of formal and informal education in Kazakhstan. Thus, in 1995-96 UNESCO played a leading role in co-ordinating an ADB funded national survey of primary, secondary, tertiary and vocational education in Kazakhstan totalling USD 890,000. In the field of science, UNESCO is implementing a major environmental monitoring project at the Aral Sea and working on problems relating to the Caspian Sea and the former nuclear testing site at Semipalatinsk. Through its regional Silk Road project UNESCO has been active in promoting cultural activities. One of the important examples is the «MOST» (Bridge) programme, which expands co-operation among Kazakhstan and international artists. Many communication development activities aimed at supporting mass media and developing journalism have also been put in place by the office since its initial year of inception. 
The main priorities of the World Health Organisation (WHO) program in Kazakhstan are the following: Reform of the health care system, Maternal and child health, Nursing reforming, National nutrition policy, Infectious diseases control, Control of non-communicable diseases, Drug policy development, and Environment and health. WHO provides technical and expert assistance based on a two-year program. WHO supports Kazakhstan to implement country Medium-term programme and inter-country activities and also woks through WHO Network. In 1996 several projects became operational in Kazakhstan, among which the MECACAR project provided Kazakhstan with 2,920,000 anti-poliomyelitis vaccines. The “Water Supply” Project in co-operation with other donors assisted central and local authorities in solution of the problems related to safe drinking water supply. Government/WHO Medium-term co-operation program for 2000-2001 is now under implementation.
Kazakhstan officially joined the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) in June 1997; UNIDO plans to open the country office in Kazakhstan in early 2000.  Nevertheless, even before joining the Organisation, UNIDO experts have implemented different projects in the country.  In November 1995, jointly with UNDP, UNIDO started the Project on “Promotion of Small and Medium Enterprises” which in its first phase provided restructuring assistance to Tekeli Lead and Zinc Company (Combinat).  In the second phase of the project a Business Advisory Centre in Almaty was established which has provided consultancy services for around 454 entrepreneurs and private enterprises and training through 38 seminars on basics of business for more that 2300 participants in Almaty, Kzylorda, Kustanai, Tekeli, Uralsk.  726 business plans were prepared by national consultants and received financing from different funds and banks.  The Almaty Business Advisory Center assisted in creation of similar centres in Tekeli and Atyrau.  UNIDO has also provided assistance to other UNDP programs and projects on Gender in Development, Aral Sea Seashore Rehabilitation and Capacity-Building, as well as with other UN agencies.
Kazakhstan joined the World Bank (WB) in July 1992. Since then, the IBRD has provided 21 loans to Kazakhstan totalling US$ 1.8 billion, of which US$ 1.1 billion have already been disbursed. In addition, the IBRD has helped mobilise co- and parallel financing from other sources. Four Consultative Group meetings for Kazakhstan held under the chairmanship of the World Bank, resulted with nearly US$ 4 billion of external assistance to Kazakhstan. Initial lending from the World Bank (Rehabilitation, Structural Adjustment and Financial Sector Adjustment Loans) has focused on supporting the Government's effort in designing and implementing structural reforms in key areas such as: privatisation, enterprise reform, financial sector reform and social protection. Once significant progress was made on the implementation of key structural reforms, the focus has begun to shift towards investment projects for deepening and fine tuning reforms (Public Sector Resource Management Adjustment and Pension Reform Adjustment Loans). In 1999 the WB approved the Road Transport Rehabilitation Project (US$100M), Health Project (US$42.5M) Legal Reform Project (US$16.5M), Atyrau Municipal Rehabilitation Project (US$16.5M) and Electricity Transmission Rehabilitation Project (US$140M). The next loan to be considered for approval is the Social Protection Adjustment Loan, which will support the Government to rationalise and streamline social assistance programs for the poor. 
The World Bank and the Government of Kazakhstan are now in the process of preparing the partnership strategy for the next three years. Consistent with the national reform objectives, the WB assistance strategy evolves around: (a) stimulating broad based growth strategy that generates employment and increases incomes outside the extractive sectors; (b) enabling a reformed public sector that effectively and efficiently delivers public services to the people; (c) supporting the most vulnerable; and (d) protecting the environment. 
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has been working in Kazakhstan since 1992 to assist the Government in implementation of macro-economic policies aimed at sharply reducing inflation and halting the collapse of economic growth. Kazakhstan received considerable technical assistance and training in virtually every area of economic policy. In addition to short-term missions, the fund provided resident advisors to the National Bank of Kazakhstan, to the State Committee for Statistics, and to the Ministry of Finance. IMF, the Government and the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK) developed a three year Extended Fund Facility program (EFF) which was approved in July 1996. That program, for USD427 million, contains structural measures aimed at redressing the structural bottlenecks of the economy. The first tranche of USD217 million was disbursed in December 1998. In December 1999 the IMF made a commitment of SDR309 million (USD453 million at the then prevailing SDR/USD exchange rate) under a three-year extended fund facility in support of the Government and the National Bank’s economic reform programme. 
The Joint United Nation Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) was established in Kazakhstan as a cosponsored programme to bring together the experience, efforts and resources of seven UN system organisations (UNICEF, UNDP, UNFPA, UNDCP, UNESCO, WHO and the World Bank) to help the world prevent new HIV infections, care for those already infected, and mitigate the impact of the epidemic. UN assistance in the field of HIV/AIDS prevention has been provided to Kazakhstan starting 1994, initially under WHO Global Programme on AIDS and since January 1996 - by UNAIDS. In Kazakhstan, UN Theme Group in collaboration with other donors (Soros, Know How, USAID) and relevant  Government sectors, initiated the multi-donor assistance Project on healthy life stile development, addressing HIV/AIDS/STD's, Drug and Reproductive Health, based on the National HLSD program. The required fund of US$ 946,300 is being mobilised, and implementation of selected priority components of the joint project is already in progress in Shymkent and Almaty cities. Number of UN/Government joint projects on HIV/AIDS/STD's and Drug abuse prevention, targeting the selected vulnerable groups in Central Asia, have been developed and became operational in 1999. 
The Office of the Department of Public Information (DPI) was opened in Kazakhstan in January 1993 to raise public awareness in objectives of the UN Global Agenda and the role and impact of the UN presence in the country. It ensures links with local media, educational institutions and NGOs, provides public information materials on the aims and activities of the UN system in political, economic, social and humanitarian fields as well as on the matters of peace and security and human rights to local audiences. In 1997-1999 together with the Soros Kazakhstan Foundation and Association of Young Leaders, a number of republican forums for high school students «The UN General Assembly Model» was held. DPI arranges special press briefings, UN related public events and meetings and also ensures the smooth running of the recently established UN Information Centre (UNIC). UNIC in Almaty serves all UN system organisations in the country and has a wide range of relevant print and video information materials about the UN. By the year 2000 UNIC will have PC workstations that will provide the access to information about the UN system through Internet to ensure better services for its numerous visitors.  
The Strategy of the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) for the Central Asian Republics and Azerbaijan concentrates on capacity building in International Economic Relations with emphasis on Trade, Investment and Finance. UNITAR has been conducting training programmes in the Central Asian Republics since 1993, within which a total of 103 representatives from public institutions in Kazakhstan have participated in training activities on international economic relations. Workshops are targeted to an audience consisting primarily of senior and medium-level public officials in charge of policy-making and technical management of economic relations. To date, 4 workshops have been conducted in Kazakhstan with the collaboration of the UNDP field office in Almaty. Funding permitting, UNITAR intends to continue its training activities in Kazakhstan (and in Central Asia in general) on Foreign Economic Relations and carry on its collaborative efforts with UNCTAD and UNDP in the field of Debt Management.
